---
title: "The physics and the numerical method"
---

This page states the equations that `stokesjx` solves, the discrete model and the
solver. The section and equation numbers follow the author's notes, and the docstrings of
the package cite the same numbers. Some numbers are therefore not used on this page
(sections 13, 14, 15 and 17).

## 1. The problem

The mantle is a spherical shell $r_c < r < R$ ($r_c = 3480$ km, $R = 6370$ km) of
viscous fluid with a radial viscosity $\eta(r)$ and a reference density $\rho_0(r)$. It
lies above an inviscid uniform core of density $\rho_c$ and below a layer of density
$\rho_w$ (water, default 0). A density anomaly $\delta\rho$ drives an instantaneous flow
$\mathbf{v}$. With the sign of the potential $\phi = -V_1$, the geoid is $N = \phi / g$,
and it is positive above a positive mass:

$$
\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} + \rho_0 \nabla\phi - \delta\rho\, g\, \hat{\mathbf{r}} = 0
\tag{1.1}
$$

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0 \ \text{(incompressible)}, \qquad
\nabla\cdot(\rho_0 \mathbf{v}) = 0 \ \text{(TALA)}
\tag{1.2}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma} = -p\,\mathbf{I} + \eta\left(\nabla\mathbf{v} + \nabla\mathbf{v}^T\right)
- \tfrac{2}{3}\eta\,(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{I}
\tag{1.3}
$$

$$
\nabla^2 \phi = -4\pi G\, \delta\rho
\tag{1.4}
$$

The flow moves no density in an instantaneous problem. So $\rho_0$ has no advection term
and is no Poisson source. The load enters only through $\delta\rho$, as sheets at the
nodes (section 7), and through the deflected boundaries (section 8). $g(r)$ is the
reference gravity (section 6). The term $\rho_0\nabla\phi$ is the self-gravitation
(section 5).

## 2. Spherical harmonics

Each field is expanded in spherical harmonics $Y = Y_{lm}$. The degree $l$ alone sets
the radial problem, with $L = l(l+1)$. The velocity is spheroidal:

$$
\mathbf{v} = u_r(r)\, Y\, \hat{\mathbf{r}} + u_t(r)\, r\nabla_1 Y
\tag{2.1}
$$

with $\nabla_1$ the gradient on the unit sphere, so $v_\theta = u_t\, \partial Y/\partial\theta$.
A kernel is a response per coefficient, so it does not depend on the normalisation of
the harmonics. The velocity kernel keeps the factor $\sqrt{L}$. The sphere average of $|\nabla_1 Y|^2$
is $L$ times that of $Y^2$. So the kernel times a density coefficient is the coefficient
of the root mean square horizontal speed. The fields follow the
conventions of lovejx.

## 3. State vector and scales

$$
\mathbf{y} = \left(u_r,\ u_t,\ \frac{r\sigma_{rr}}{\eta_s},\ \frac{r\sigma_{r\theta}}{\eta_s},\
\frac{\rho_s r \phi}{\eta_s},\ \frac{\rho_s r^2\, \partial_r\phi}{\eta_s}\right)
\tag{3.1}
$$

with $\sigma_{rr} = S_{rr} Y$ and $\sigma_{r\theta} = S\,\partial Y/\partial\theta$. All six
components are in m/s. $\eta_s$ and $\rho_s$ are scales (CODE-A: $10^{19}$ Pa s and
4500 kg/m³; the package uses the largest node viscosity for $\eta_s$). The matrix of the
radial system depends on $\eta/\eta_s$ and $\rho_0/\rho_s$ only:

$$
A = A(l,\ \eta/\eta_s,\ \rho_0/\rho_s,\ \kappa)
\tag{3.2}
$$

The scales cancel in every SI output (section 11).

## 4. The matrix A

The radial system is $d\mathbf{y}/d\ln r = A\mathbf{y}$ (Corrieu, Thoraval and Ricard
1995). With $e = \eta/\eta_s$, $d = \rho_0/\rho_s$ and $\kappa = r\, d\ln\rho_0/dr$, the six
rows are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{(a)}\quad & dy_1 = -(2+\kappa)\,y_1 + L\,y_2 \\
\text{(b)}\quad & dy_2 = -y_1 + y_2 + y_4/e \\
\text{(c)}\quad & dy_3 = 4(3+\kappa)\,e\,y_1 - 6L\,e\,y_2 + y_3 + L\,y_4 - d\,y_6 \\
\text{(d)}\quad & dy_4 = -2(3+\kappa)\,e\,y_1 + 2(2L-1)\,e\,y_2 - y_3 - 2y_4 - d\,y_5 \\
\text{(e)}\quad & dy_5 = y_5 + y_6 \\
\text{(f)}\quad & dy_6 = L\,y_5
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.1}
$$

Row (a) is the continuity equation (1.2). Row (b) is the definition of the shear stress.
Rows (c) and (d) are the radial and the tangential component of (1.1), with the pressure
eliminated. Rows (e) and (f) are (1.4) inside an interval, where there is no source. A
symbolic derivation of $A$ from (1.1) to (1.4) is a test of the package.

The term $-\tfrac{2}{3}\eta\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}$ of (1.3) cancels in the radial row and
only redefines $p$ in the tangential row. So $A$ is the same with and without it.

**TALA.** Under the truncated anelastic liquid approximation,

$$
A = A_0 + \kappa K
\tag{4.2}
$$

$$
K = \frac{\partial A}{\partial\kappa}:\quad K_{11} = -1,\quad K_{31} = 4e,\quad K_{41} = -2e,
\quad \text{all other entries } 0
\tag{4.3}
$$

$K = \mathbf{v}\,\mathbf{e}_1^T$ with $\mathbf{e}_1^T\mathbf{v} = -1$, so $K^2 = -K$ and
$\exp(Kt) = I + K(1 - e^{-t})$.

**Block structure.** In the order (mechanics, potential), $A$ is block upper triangular.
Rows 1 to 4 contain $y_5$ and $y_6$ (self-gravitation). Rows 5 and 6 contain no
mechanical unknown. The eigenvalues of the incompressible $A$ are $l+1$ (double), $l-1$,
$-l$ (double) and $-l-2$.

**Viscosity similarity.** With $D = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, e, e, e, e)$:

$$
A(e) = D\,A(1)\,D^{-1},\qquad K(e) = D\,K(1)\,D^{-1},\qquad
\exp\left(A h + K\kappa_h\right) = D\,E\,D^{-1}
\tag{4.5}
$$

where $E = \exp(A(1)\,h + K(1)\,\kappa_h)$ depends on $l$, $h$, $\rho_0/\rho_s$ and $\kappa_h$
only. A derivative with respect to $\log e$ never passes through the exponential.

**Degree balancing.** With $S_l = \mathrm{diag}(1,\ l,\ 1/(2l),\ 1/2,\ 1/2,\ 1/(2l))$,

$$
B = S_l\, A(1)\, S_l^{-1}
\tag{4.6}
$$

has entries of at most about $2(l+1)$, and its 1-norm is below $3l + 10 + d$.

## 5. Gravity levels

- **FULL**: the density entries of the self-gravitation are
  $$
  a_{36} = a_{45} = -\rho_0/\rho_s
  \tag{5.1}
  $$
  The core pressure $\rho_c\phi$ enters the CMB condition (8.4, 8.5), and the water term
  $\rho_w\phi$ enters the surface topography (8.3).
- **NO_SELF_GRAVITY**: all three terms are zero:
  $$
  a_{36} = a_{45} = 0,\qquad \rho_c\phi \to 0,\qquad \rho_w\phi \to 0
  \tag{5.2}
  $$
  The geoid is still computed from the load and the two boundary sheets. Rows 5 and 6
  and the potential conditions (8.2) and (8.5) stay, but they no longer act on the
  mechanics.

## 6. Background gravity

$$
g(r_i) = \frac{G}{r_i^2}\left(M_c + \sum_{k \le i} \tfrac{4\pi}{3}\,\bar\rho_k\left(r_k^3 - r_{k-1}^3\right)\right)
\tag{6.1}
$$

with $\bar\rho_k$ the interval mean of the node densities and $M_c$ the core mass (by
default the consistent value $\tfrac{4\pi}{3}r_c^3\rho_c$). A shell of constant density is
exact for the discrete model, and a jump pair adds no mass. $g$ enters only at nodes:
in the source jump (7.1) and in the sheet masses of section 8. The uniform alternative is

$$
g = g_0
\tag{6.2}
$$

which `assess` (with $g_0 = 1$) and the G-ADOPT benchmark use.

## 7. Source

A sheet of surface density $\sigma$ (kg/m², per unit harmonic coefficient) at the node
$r_s$ gives the jump of the state:

$$
[y_3] = \frac{r_s\, g(r_s)\, \sigma}{\eta_s},\qquad
[y_6] = -\frac{4\pi G\, r_s^2\, \rho_s\, \sigma}{\eta_s}
\tag{7.1}
$$

The stress below the sheet carries its weight, and the potential gradient jumps by the
attraction of the sheet. A kernel is the response to $\sigma = 1$ in one harmonic.

A sheet at an end node is compensated statically with no flow. For every degree,
viscosity, boundary class, gravity level and compressibility:

$$
h_s(R) = -\frac{1}{\rho_0(R) - \rho_w},\qquad
h_c(r_c) = \frac{1}{\rho_0(r_c) - \rho_c},\qquad
N = u_t = 0 \ \text{at both end nodes}
\tag{7.2}
$$

## 8. Boundary conditions

**Mechanics.** $u_r = 0$ at both boundaries. Free slip sets $\sigma_{r\theta} = 0$, and no
slip sets $u_t = 0$:

$$
y_1 = 0,\qquad y_4 = 0\ \text{(free slip)}\quad\text{or}\quad y_2 = 0\ \text{(no slip)}
\tag{8.1}
$$

**Surface potential.** Above $R$ the potential is $\alpha r^l + \beta r^{-(l+1)}$. The total
surface mass is the sheet of the deflected surface plus the water sheet that follows the
geoid. With (8.3) it is $-\sigma_{rr}/g(R)$ for every $\rho_w$. Without an applied field
($\alpha = 0$), the jump of $\partial_r\phi$ across this sheet gives the raw row

$$
y_6 + (l+1)\,y_5 + c_s\,y_3 = 0,\qquad c_s = \frac{4\pi G R \rho_s}{g(R)}
\tag{8.2}
$$

**Surface topography.** The water surface follows the total equipotential:

$$
h_s = -\frac{\sigma_{rr} + \rho_w\phi}{(\rho_{top} - \rho_w)\, g(R)}
\tag{8.3}
$$

$\rho_{top}$ is the density of the top node. PREM has 1020 or 2600 kg/m³ there, depending
on its ocean layer, so the profile carries $\rho_{top}$ as a field of its own.

**CMB.** The core is uniform and inviscid, with the pressure $p_c = \rho_c\phi$ (FULL)
and an interior potential proportional to $r^l$:

$$
h_c = -\frac{\sigma_{rr} + \rho_c\phi}{(\rho_0(r_c) - \rho_c)\, g(r_c)}
\tag{8.4}
$$

$$
y_6 = l\,y_5 - c_c\left(y_3 + \frac{\rho_c}{\rho_s}\,y_5\right),\qquad
c_c = \frac{4\pi G r_c \rho_s}{g(r_c)}
\tag{8.5}
$$

$h_c$ is the outward-positive deflection. NO_SELF_GRAVITY drops $\rho_c\phi$.

**Core model.** The gravity needs the mass below the CMB, and the CMB condition needs
$\rho_c$. The default is the consistent core, $M_c = \tfrac{4\pi}{3}r_c^3\rho_c$. A core mass
that differs from this value is a "split core", for example the PREM core mass with
$\rho_c = 9900$ kg/m³. A split core does not conserve momentum at degree 1 (section 10).

## 9. Outputs and units

The kernels per unit sheet density, in SI units:

$$
N = \frac{\eta_s\, y_5(R)}{\rho_s\, R\, g(R)} \quad \text{(m per kg/m²)}
\tag{9.1}
$$

$$
h_s = \text{(8.3) with } \sigma_{rr} = \eta_s\, y_3(R)/R \quad \text{(m per kg/m²)}
\tag{9.2}
$$

$$
h_c = \text{(8.4) at } r_c \quad \text{(m per kg/m²)}
\tag{9.3}
$$

$$
u_t(R)\,\sqrt{L} \quad \text{(m/s per kg/m²)}
\tag{9.4}
$$

Under a no-slip surface the surface velocity is zero by construction. The dimensionless
geoid kernel of Hager and Clayton (1989), per unit $\delta\rho\, dr$, is
$G_l = (2l+1)\, g N / (4\pi G R)$ with $N$ of (9.1).

## 10. Degree 1

At $l = 1$ the radial system can be singular, and its solutions then differ by a
translation-like state. The package selects one member by a static rule.

**(a)** Take FULL with hydrostatic gravity and a consistent core. The internal forces then
sum to zero for every state, and the whole-body force balance at $l = 1$ is an identity:

$$
a\, y_4(R) + b\, p(R) + c\, y_4(r_c) = 0,\qquad p = y_6 + (l+1)\,y_5 + c_s\,y_3
\tag{10.1}
$$

With free slip at both boundaries, $y_4 = 0$ at both, so $p = 0$ for every state, and the
raw system is singular for every mantle density profile. With a no-slip boundary, the
anchor carries no force, and the raw solution is a member of the free-slip family. For a
uniform density no solution exists.

**(b)** For a uniform mantle density the null vector is the rigid translation. For a
density that varies with the radius it is a state with flow, because the equations have no
advection of $\rho_0$.

**(c)** A move of the origin by $d$ along the axis of the harmonic changes the three
outputs by $d$. It changes the load by the sheets of the moved density jumps. A shift of the
outputs alone is a change of origin only for a uniform density.

**(d)** In the singular case the solutions are $\mathbf{s} + c\,\mathbf{n}$. The
centre-of-mass (CM) frame is the member whose self-potential has no degree-1 term,
$N_1 = 0$. All four outputs come from this member, and its geoid at $l = 1$ is zero.

**(e)** Above the surface the degree-1 potential is $\alpha r + \beta r^{-2}$. The raw row
sets $\alpha = 0$; the CM row sets $\beta = 0$ and leaves $\alpha$ free:

$$
y_6 - l\,y_5 + c_s\,y_3 = 0 \qquad (l = 1)
\tag{10.5}
$$

The uniform field $\alpha r Y_1$ is the d'Alembert force of the frame of the centre of
mass. With a split core the model does not conserve momentum, and the CM row adds the
uniform field that keeps the centre of mass at the origin. Its size is reported as

$$
I_{\mathrm{imb}} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{eff}}\, A}{\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\, g(r_s)\, r_s^2},\qquad
A = \phi_a(R)/R,\qquad M_{\mathrm{eff}} = M_{\mathrm{mantle}} + \tfrac{4\pi}{3}r_c^3\rho_c
\tag{10.6}
$$

the uniform force on the whole body over the gravity force on the unit load sheet
(`Kernels.degree_one_imbalance`).

**(f)** The frame follows from the flags, the boundary classes and the core model, never
from a numerical value:

| Configuration at `l = 1` | Raw system | Offered | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| FULL, hydrostatic `g`, free slip at both, consistent core | singular | CM | CM |
| the same, split core | not singular | CM, raw | CM |
| FULL, hydrostatic `g`, a no-slip boundary, consistent core | singular for a uniform density, otherwise a member of the free-slip family | none | refused |
| the same, split core | not singular, value set by the core split | raw on explicit request only | refused |
| NO_SELF_GRAVITY, or uniform `g` | not singular | raw | raw |

Where degree 1 is refused, the kernels start at `l = 2`.

## 11. Invariances

- The scales $\rho_s$ and $\eta_s$ cancel in every SI output.
- $\eta \to c\,\eta$ leaves the geoid and the topographies unchanged and divides the
  velocity by $c$.
- The outputs are linear in the load: a kernel is the response to a unit sheet.

## 12. The discrete model

The radial model is a node table, CMB first. Two equal neighbouring radii are a jump
pair (an interval of zero width).

The material of an interval is the mean of its two nodes:

$$
\bar\eta_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(\eta_{i-1} + \eta_i),\qquad \bar\rho_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(\rho_{0,i-1} + \rho_{0,i})
\tag{12.1}
$$

The interval step is exact for this material:

$$
P_i = \exp\left(A_0(\bar\eta_i, \bar\rho_i)\, h_i + K(\bar\eta_i)\, \kappa_{h,i}\right),\qquad
h_i = \ln(r_i/r_{i-1}),\qquad \kappa_{h,i} = \ln(\rho_{0,i}/\rho_{0,i-1})
\tag{12.2}
$$

There is no division by $h_i$, and the step is exact for a power law
$\rho_0 \propto r^\kappa$ inside the interval. $A$ is constant in an interval, because $g$
does not enter $A$.

Under TALA the step across a jump pair is the anelastic rule, the $h \to 0$ limit of
(12.2):

$$
P_{\text{pair}} = I + K(\bar\eta)\left(1 - \frac{\rho_{0,-}}{\rho_{0,+}}\right)
\tag{12.3}
$$

$\rho_0 u_r$ is continuous across the pair, and $u_r$ jumps. The density jumps of $\rho_0$
in the mantle are phase changes: the material crosses them, so the mass flux is
continuous. In the incompressible model the pair step is the identity.

The fields use the trapezoid weights of the node table:

$$
w_j = \tfrac{1}{2}(\Delta_j + \Delta_{j+1}),\qquad \Delta_i = (r_i - r_{i-1})\, m_i,\qquad
\Delta_0 = \Delta_N = 0
\tag{12.4}
$$

with the static mask $m_i$ (0 at a pair, 1 elsewhere). The weights sum to $R - r_c$, and
each node of a pair takes the half interval on its own side.

Under TALA the exponent assumes a power law inside an interval, while the force terms and
$g$ use the interval mean. On a smooth table (cubic density, smooth viscosity) the
measured order of convergence in the node spacing is 2.0 to 2.3.

## 16. The solver

**Coordinates.** The sweep variable is $\mathbf{z} = S_l\mathbf{y}$ with $S_l$ of (4.6),
and $\eta_s$ is the largest node viscosity. With $e_i = \bar\eta_i/\eta_s$ and
$D_i = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, e_i, e_i, e_i, e_i)$ the step of interval $i$ is

$$
Z_i = D_i\, E_i\, D_i^{-1},\qquad E_i = \exp(B_i),\qquad
B_i = S_l\left(A(1, d_i)\, h_i + K(1)\, \kappa_{h,i}\right) S_l^{-1}
\tag{16.1}
$$

**The exponentials.** The steps and their inverses come from one diagonal Pade
approximant of order $m$ with scaling and squaring. The approximant satisfies
$r_m(-X) = r_m(X)^{-1}$ exactly, so one set of powers gives both $E_i$ and $E_i^{-1}$.
The order and the squaring count are static. They come from a static bound of the scaled
1-norm, which the configuration computes from the limits of the node table. The
accuracy thresholds of the scaled 1-norm are 0.950 for order 7 and 2.098 for order 9
(Higham 2005). At these thresholds the backward error bound
$|\log(e^{-x} r_m(x))|/x$ equals the unit roundoff $2^{-53}$. For order 6 the threshold
0.783 is a choice of this package, with the bound 9.3e-15. The plan of the package never
selects order 6, because order 7 costs the same four matrix products and allows a larger
norm.

The Pade denominators are solved by elimination without pivoting. If the scalar Pade
numerator satisfies $N_m(x) < 2$ at the scaled bound $x$, both denominators are strictly
diagonally dominant by columns. Elimination without pivoting is then stable, with a
growth factor of at most 2 (Higham 2002). The static plan enforces this condition.

**Sweeps.** The upward sweep starts from the CMB basis of (8.1) and (8.5). The downward
sweep starts from the surface basis of (8.1) and (8.2), or of (10.5) in the CM frame. After
each step the three columns are orthonormalised by classical Gram-Schmidt with one
re-orthogonalisation. For columns of numerical full rank this keeps them orthonormal to
working precision (Giraud et al. 2005, Theorem 2).

**Row carry.** The outputs are linear functionals of the state at the surface and at the
CMB. Each output row is carried through the triangular factors of the Gram-Schmidt steps,
so the rows shrink where the basis grows. A kernel underflows only where it is below
1e-308 of its scale ($l$ above about 1100).

**Node system.** At node $j$ the state below the sheet satisfies the CMB conditions, and
the state above it satisfies the surface conditions. Their difference is the jump of
(7.1):

$$
\left[-Q^{\text{up}}_j,\ Q^{\text{dn}}_j\right]
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{a}\\ \mathbf{b}\end{pmatrix} = S_l\,\mathbf{J}_j
\tag{16.4}
$$

one 6×6 system per degree and node, all solved in one batched call.

## 18. Fields

A field coefficient is the radial integral of a kernel times the density anomaly, with
the trapezoid weights of (12.4):

$$
F_o[l, m] = \sum_j K_o[l, j]\; w_j\; \delta\rho[j, l, m]
\tag{18.2}
$$

A kernel in m (or m/s) per kg/m², times a weight in m, times a density in kg/m³, gives
m (or m/s). `fields.apply` and `fields.radial_integral` compute (18.2).

The free-air gravity anomaly (`fields.gravity_anomaly`) is

$$
\Delta g_l = f_l\, \frac{g(R)\, N_l}{R},\qquad f_l = l - 1\ (l \ge 1),\qquad f_0 = 0
\tag{18.3}
$$

in m/s². The same $g(R)$ divides the potential in (9.1), so $\Delta g_l = f_l\,\phi_l/R$ for
every background.

The admittance (`fields.admittance`) is

$$
Z_l = \frac{S_{gh}(l)}{S_{hh}(l)},\qquad
S_{xy}(l) = \sum_m \left(C^x_{lm}C^y_{lm} + S^x_{lm}S^y_{lm}\right)
\tag{18.4}
$$

in the real conventions, and $\sum_m w_m \mathrm{Re}(x_{lm}\overline{y_{lm}})$ with $w_0 = 1$,
$w_{m>0} = 2$ in `complex_4pi`. The result is 0 where $S_{hh} = 0$. Units: s⁻²
(1 mGal/km = 1e-8 s⁻²). $Z_l$ does not depend on the convention.

## 19. The viscosity cut

A viscosity cut is a viscosity jump at a radius $c$ inside one interval of a fixed node
table. It is not a node pair. With $r_a \le c < r_{a+1}$, interval $a$ has the viscosity
$e_{lo} = \eta_a/\eta_s$ below $c$ and $e_{hi} = \eta_{a+1}/\eta_s$ above it, and the
material of the whole interval. With the balanced exponent $B_a$ of the interval and the
fractions $f_{lo} = \ln(c/r_a)/h_a$ and $f_{hi} = \ln(r_{a+1}/c)/h_a$:

$$
Z_{\text{cut}} = D(e_{hi})\, \exp(f_{hi} B_a)\, D(e_{hi})^{-1}\; D(e_{lo})\, \exp(f_{lo} B_a)\, D(e_{lo})^{-1}
\tag{19.1}
$$

Every other interval keeps (12.1) to (12.3). The gravity, the jump vectors, the boundary
rows and the outputs do not depend on the cut. A cut on a node ($c = r_a$) gives a lower
part of zero width, whose step is the identity exactly.

The cut model equals a concrete node table exactly in some cases. An example is an
incompressible formulation with a pair at $c$ whose lower member carries $\rho_{0,a+1}$
and whose upper member carries $\rho_{0,a}$. Each part of interval $a$ then has the
interval mean $\tfrac{1}{2}(\rho_{0,a} + \rho_{0,a+1})$ of the density, as in the cut.
Under an incompressible formulation the map from $c$ to every output is
continuously differentiable, also where the cut crosses a node or a density pair. Under
TALA the kernels jump when the cut crosses a density pair ([derivatives](gradients.qmd)).
